title: Type 2 Diabetes: Diagnose Correctly, Then Build Risk-Based Initial Care
bottomLine: Diagnose diabetes using accepted Canadian laboratory criteria and confirm an abnormal result in an asymptomatic person. At diagnosis, classify the likely diabetes type, look for metabolic decompensation, establish cardiovascular/kidney risk and start treatment that fits both glycemia and comorbidity rather than reflexively prescribing the same first drug to everyone.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, blurred vision and recurrent infection increase concern for symptomatic hyperglycemia.
Lean phenotype, ketosis, rapid progression, autoimmune history or marked catabolic symptoms should raise concern for type 1/LADA or another diabetes form rather than routine type 2 diabetes.
differentiate: A1C can be unreliable when red-cell turnover or hemoglobin conditions are abnormal; glucose-based testing is preferred when A1C accuracy is doubtful.
Stress hyperglycemia during acute illness is not automatically chronic type 2 diabetes.
assessment: Assess symptoms, weight trajectory, pregnancy, medications such as glucocorticoids/antipsychotics, family history, BP, smoking, cardiovascular disease, kidney disease, neuropathy/foot symptoms and access to food/medications.
workup: Use fasting plasma glucose, A1C, OGTT or random plasma glucose according to the clinical context and Diabetes Canada diagnostic criteria.
Assess kidney function/albuminuria, lipids and other baseline cardiovascular/complication measures appropriate to age and disease context.
management: Start health-behaviour support and individualized pharmacotherapy; metformin remains an initial agent for most adults who require medication, while specific SGLT2 inhibitors and/or GLP-1 receptor agonists are prioritized when cardiorenal indications exist.
Use insulin immediately when metabolic decompensation, ketosis, hyperosmolar state or severe symptomatic hyperglycemia makes non-insulin sequencing unsafe.
medicationSafety: Choose therapy with renal function, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, adverse-effect profile, cost/coverage and cardiorenal disease in mind.
Do not use A1C alone to justify intensification when recurrent hypoglycemia or frailty makes a lower target unsafe.
redFlags: Hyperosmolar dehydration or altered mental status
counselling: Explain diagnosis and treatment without blame and distinguish long-term glycemic goals from immediate safety issues.
Discuss cardiorenal protection when a medication is recommended despite an A1C already near target.
followUp: Review glycemia, medication tolerance/access and baseline complication screening promptly after diagnosis and treatment initiation.
examTrap: Delaying insulin in catabolic or ketotic severe hyperglycemia because the patient is presumed to have type 2 diabetes.
oneLinePearl: Confirm asymptomatic diabetes; treat metabolic decompensation immediately and choose long-term therapy for the whole risk profile.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Definition, Classification and Diagnosis
Diabetes Canada Pharmacologic Glycemic Management of Type 2 Diabetes in Adults — 2024 Update

title: Type 1 Diabetes: Basal Insulin Is Essential, Regimens Must Match Physiology
bottomLine: Type 1 diabetes is absolute insulin deficiency. A safe regimen provides continuous basal insulin plus meal/correction insulin through multiple daily injections or pump therapy; fasting, illness or NPO status can change doses but does not remove the physiologic need for basal insulin.
recognize: Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, ketosis or DKA may be the first presentation.
Pump interruption can create rapid insulin deficiency because there is no long-acting depot.
differentiate: Type 2 diabetes can also present with ketosis and some adults have autoimmune diabetes with slower progression; classification may require antibodies/C-peptide when the phenotype is unclear.
Basal insulin covers background hepatic glucose output; prandial insulin covers meals and correction insulin addresses unexpected hyperglycemia.
assessment: Review regimen, CGM/pump data, hypoglycemia, ketones, meal pattern, exercise, injection/infusion sites, sick-day knowledge and psychosocial burden.
workup: Use A1C and glucose/CGM data for chronic management; use ketone/electrolyte/acid-base evaluation urgently when DKA is possible.
Screen associated autoimmune and microvascular disease according to age/duration/current Diabetes Canada guidance.
management: Use individualized basal-bolus or pump/automated-delivery therapy with carbohydrate/meal planning and structured education.
During acute illness or fasting, preserve basal insulin while adjusting prandial/correction therapy according to the clinical plan and monitoring more frequently.
medicationSafety: Never omit basal insulin entirely in type 1 diabetes without an appropriate replacement strategy.
Have a backup insulin plan for pump failure and verify insulin concentration/device before dose changes.
counselling: Teach sick-day rules, ketone testing, hypoglycemia rescue, pump-failure backup and safe exercise/meal adjustment.
followUp: Use diabetes-team support and reassess time in range, hypoglycemia, regimen burden and device access rather than focusing on A1C alone.
examTrap: Holding all insulin because a person with type 1 diabetes is NPO.
oneLinePearl: No food may reduce prandial insulin; it never makes basal insulin optional in type 1 diabetes.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Glycemic Management in Adults With Type 1 Diabetes
Diabetes Canada Type 1 Diabetes / CGM safety resources

title: DKA: Fluids, Potassium, Insulin, Ketone Clearance, and the Cause
bottomLine: DKA is a metabolic emergency defined by ketosis and acidosis, not merely high glucose. Restore volume/perfusion, know potassium before insulin, clear ketoacidosis with protocolized insulin and dextrose as needed, monitor frequently and treat the precipitating cause; SGLT2-associated or pregnancy DKA can occur with only modest glucose elevation.
recognize: Polyuria/polydipsia, dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, altered mental status and ketones support DKA.
Common precipitants include missed insulin, infection, new diabetes, MI/stroke, surgery/trauma and medications including SGLT2 inhibitors.
differentiate: Starvation/alcoholic ketosis and lactic acidosis can overlap; use beta-hydroxybutyrate, anion gap and clinical context.
Urine ketones can underestimate beta-hydroxybutyrate-predominant DKA and should not falsely reassure.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, dehydration, infection/ischemia symptoms, pregnancy and insulin/SGLT2 exposure.
Obtain ECG when important potassium disturbance is plausible.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, ketones/beta-hydroxybutyrate, venous/arterial acid-base testing as appropriate and anion gap; investigate the precipitant with targeted tests.
management: Use a validated DKA protocol for crystalloid fluid resuscitation, potassium-guided insulin therapy, dextrose when needed to continue clearing ketosis and frequent biochemical reassessment.
With severe hypokalemia, correct potassium before insulin because insulin can worsen intracellular potassium shift.
Continue therapy until ketoacidosis resolves clinically/biochemically rather than stopping when glucose alone normalizes.
medicationSafety: SGLT2-associated DKA can occur without marked hyperglycemia.
Avoid routine bicarbonate except in the extreme-acidosis situations defined by the active protocol/guideline.
counselling: After recovery, review sick-day rules, ketone testing, insulin continuity and SGLT2 peri-illness/surgery safety where relevant.
followUp: Close the loop on the precipitating cause, insulin/medication access and prompt diabetes follow-up before discharge.
examTrap: Stopping DKA treatment because glucose normalized while ketones/anion-gap acidosis persists—or excluding DKA because glucose is not extremely high.
oneLinePearl: DKA ends when ketoacidosis resolves, not when the glucose looks better.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults
Diabetes Canada 2025 Type 1 Diabetes update where applicable

title: HHS: Restore Perfusion and Correct Hyperosmolality Carefully
bottomLine: HHS is profound hyperglycemic hyperosmolality with severe water deficit and relatively little ketoacidosis. It is often a disease of older or medically vulnerable adults; restore perfusion, replace fluid/electrolyte deficits carefully, use insulin within the validated protocol and avoid rapid osmotic correction while treating the precipitant.
recognize: Marked dehydration, extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality and altered consciousness are characteristic; neurologic symptoms may mimic stroke or seizure disease.
Infection is a common precipitant, but MI, stroke, surgery, glucocorticoids/diuretics and poor access to water/medication also contribute.
differentiate: HHS has more profound hyperosmolality/dehydration and less prominent ketoacidosis than classic DKA, but mixed DKA/HHS can occur.
Coma is not required; the older term hyperosmolar nonketotic coma is misleading.
assessment: Assess ABCs, mental status, perfusion, volume depletion, infection/ischemia/stroke clues, medications, kidney/cardiac disease and baseline functional/cognitive status.
workup: Use glucose, electrolytes, corrected sodium/effective osmolality, creatinine, ketones/acid-base testing and cause-directed studies; monitor neurologic status and fluid balance closely.
management: Use a validated HHS protocol with individualized crystalloid replacement, potassium management, insulin and careful osmolality decline.
Avoid fixed aggressive fluid treatment in frail heart/kidney disease without repeated perfusion/volume reassessment.
Treat the precipitating condition and thrombosis/aspiration/renal complications when present.
medicationSafety: Rapid osmotic shifts can cause neurologic harm; insulin and fluids can rapidly change potassium and sodium balance.
Medication-related contributors such as glucocorticoids/diuretics require review after stabilization.
counselling: After recovery, address hydration access, medication adherence, sick-day planning and caregiver support when cognition/frailty contributed.
followUp: Ensure diabetes regimen and social/access causes are corrected before discharge and arrange prompt follow-up.
examTrap: Treating HHS as 'DKA with a higher glucose' and correcting water/osmolality too rapidly without considering frailty or heart/kidney disease.
oneLinePearl: HHS is primarily a profound water/osmolality emergency—resuscitate deliberately and reassess often.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hyperglycemic Emergencies in Adults

title: Hypoglycemia: Correct the Low, Then Prevent the Next One
bottomLine: Hypoglycemia is a treatment emergency first and a medication-safety investigation second. Correct the low according to severity, then identify insulin/secretagogue timing, meals, activity, alcohol, kidney function, frailty, food insecurity or hypoglycemia unawareness that made recurrence likely.
recognize: Autonomic symptoms include tremor, sweating, hunger and palpitations; neuroglycopenia can cause confusion, behaviour change, seizure or unconsciousness.
Older adults may present with falls, delirium or weakness and have less reliable adrenergic warning.
differentiate: A person able to swallow can use oral fast-acting carbohydrate; severe hypoglycemia with inability to self-treat requires external rescue with glucagon or IV glucose according to the setting.
Sulfonylurea and long-acting insulin hypoglycemia can recur after initial correction.
assessment: Check glucose without delaying treatment when severe symptoms are present; assess airway/swallow safety, injury, seizure and medication exposure.
Review insulin/secretagogue doses, missed meals, exercise, alcohol, renal/hepatic disease, acute illness, weight loss and food access.
workup: For recurrent unexplained hypoglycemia without an obvious diabetes-medication cause, investigate endocrine, hepatic, renal or other causes according to the clinical pattern rather than ordering a universal panel.
management: Treat conscious self-treatable hypoglycemia with approximately 15 g fast-acting glucose/carbohydrate and recheck in about 10-15 minutes, repeating when still low according to Diabetes Canada guidance.
Use glucagon or IV glucose for severe episodes depending on access/setting, then provide longer-acting carbohydrate/meal when appropriate.
Reduce or redesign the causative regimen and individualize targets when recurrent/severe hypoglycemia occurs.
medicationSafety: Insulin and sulfonylureas require active hypoglycemia prevention, especially with CKD, frailty, irregular intake and cognitive impairment.
High-risk patients/supports should have glucagon education/access when appropriate.
counselling: Teach fast-carbohydrate treatment, rechecking, driving safety, glucagon and the individual reasons this episode occurred.
followUp: Any severe episode requires prompt medication/target review; use CGM or diabetes-team support when it will reduce recurrence.
examTrap: Treating a low successfully and making no change to the medication pattern that caused it.
oneLinePearl: A corrected glucose ends the episode; preventing recurrence completes the care.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Hypoglycemia in Adults — 2023 Update

title: Hypothyroidism: TSH-First Primary Disease, Free T4 for Central Disease and Special Contexts
bottomLine: For suspected primary hypothyroidism, TSH is the preferred first-line test; free T4 becomes important when TSH is abnormal or central/pituitary disease makes TSH unreliable. Levothyroxine dosing is individualized to age, weight, pregnancy, coronary disease, severity and absorption/adherence rather than adjusted from symptoms alone.
recognize: Fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, menstrual change and bradycardia are nonspecific and require biochemical confirmation.
Myxedema coma is systemic decompensation with altered consciousness, hypothermia, hypoventilation or severe cardiovascular/metabolic dysfunction—not merely a very high TSH.
differentiate: High TSH plus low free T4 supports overt primary hypothyroidism; low free T4 with an inappropriately normal/low TSH suggests central disease.
Non-thyroidal illness, assay interference and medications can distort testing.
assessment: Review pregnancy, cardiac disease, pituitary symptoms, amiodarone/lithium, supplements/biotin, adherence and timing relative to food/iron/calcium.
workup: Use TSH first in most primary-thyroid presentations; add free T4 as indicated and use antibodies selectively when etiology matters.
Do not routinely use free T4/T3 to titrate stable primary hypothyroidism when TSH is reliable.
management: Use levothyroxine replacement and titrate to TSH for primary disease, with cautious initiation in frail older adults/significant coronary disease and more intensive pregnancy monitoring.
Central hypothyroidism requires specialist/pituitary context and free-T4-guided management; address possible adrenal insufficiency first when relevant.
medicationSafety: Iron, calcium and several medications impair levothyroxine absorption; overtreatment increases atrial-fibrillation and bone risk.
Do not start thyroid replacement before addressing possible significant central adrenal insufficiency.
redFlags: Possible adrenal insufficiency before thyroid therapy
counselling: Teach consistent dosing and separation from interfering supplements/medications; explain why symptom changes alone do not justify repeated rapid dose changes.
followUp: Recheck thyroid function after meaningful dose changes at an interval that allows steady state; pregnancy needs earlier/frequent review.
examTrap: Calling a low free T4 normal because TSH is normal in a patient with pituitary disease—or repeatedly adjusting stable primary hypothyroidism from free T3 testing.
oneLinePearl: TSH governs most primary hypothyroidism; central disease is the major exception.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada / Canadian Society of Endocrinology and Metabolism Endocrinology Recommendations — updated April 2026
